Prevention: Bury plant debris, eliminate volunteer onion plants, and remove cull piles, all of which can be sources of the pathogen.
Rotate to non-hosts (small grains, corn) for at least three years.

To minimize high humidity, plant in the direction of prevailing winds, avoid using wind breaks, and manage plant density and spacing.
Avoid overhead irrigation as downy mildew spores forms of onion active at night, when the leaves are wet.
Monitoring: Rain is not needed for infection.
Check for dew during the night and morning hours as (1.5 to 7 hours of leaf wetness and 6° to 26°C) are favourable for the development of disease.
The fungus overwinters in volunteer hosts, cull, piles, and debris.
Downey mildew first attacks the older leaves and rapidly destroys the foliage.
Temperatures between 10 to 12°C are most favorable, although the disease can develop at temperatures between 4°C to 25°C.
Direct Control: The diseased plants should be removed and burnt soon after being detected in the field.

Dry-heat treatment of bulbs at 40°C for 8 hours favours the destruction of any internal mycelium (fungus).

However, do these sanitation practices when the plants are not wet to prevent the further spread of the disease.
Restrictions: Always wear impermeable gloves, long pants & long-sleeve shirts during spray.
Change clothes and wash your hands immediately after applying pesticides.
Don't spray outdoors on windy or rainy days.
Fungicides may be applied on a 7-day schedule, if necessary.
For all fungicides, thorough coverage of foliage is important for the control disease.
